sec.title: Background
sec.p: Relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma treatment is challenging. Bispecific antibodies targeting B-cell maturation antigens, including elranatamab and teclistamab, have demonstrated encouraging responses in heavily pretreated diseases. Nonetheless, comparative data from real-world practice are limited.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: This study aimed to compare the time to the next treatment, overall survival, and adverse events in patients with refractory multiple myeloma receiving elranatamab or teclistamab monotherapy in real-world practice.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted a multinational retrospective cohort study using deidentified electronic health records from the TriNetX Global Research Network. Adults with refractory multiple myeloma receiving elranatamab or teclistamab as monotherapy after one or more prior systemic regimen were included. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed based on demographics, comorbidities, and baseline laboratory values. The primary endpoint was the time to the next treatment. Secondary endpoints were overall survival and safety outcomes, including cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, cytopenia, and infections.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Following matching, 188 patients were included in each group. The median time to the next treatment did not differ significantly between elranatamab and teclistamab (11.0 vs 12.3 months; p = 0.394), and the 3-year overall survival rates were similar (58.8% vs 59.7%; p = 0.077). Subgroup analyses indicated a longer time to the next treatment with teclistamab in patients with baseline thrombocytopenia and in those receiving more than five prior lines of treatment. Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia was more frequent with teclistamab (84.6% vs 74.5%; p = 0.015), whereas cytokine release syndrome occurred more often with elranatamab (45.2% vs 27.1%; p < 0.001). The immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome and infection rates were comparable. Both agents demonstrated comparable real-world effectiveness but different toxicity profiles.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These findings support individualized treatment selection; prospective comparative trials are warranted.

tr.td: In a real-world propensity score-matched cohort, elranatamab and teclistamab demonstrated comparable effectiveness in refractory multiple myeloma, with no significant differences in the time to the next treatment or overall survival, although teclistamab showed a longer time to the next treatment in selected high-risk subgroups.

The two B-cell maturation antigen bispecific antibodies exhibited distinct safety profiles, with higher rates of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia observed with teclistamab and more frequent cytokine release syndrome with elranatamab, supporting individualized treatment selection in clinical practice.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a hematological cancer characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal plasma cells. Frequent clinical manifestations include anemia, skeletal pain, impaired renal function, and elevated serum calcium levels. The worldwide MM incidence continues to increase, with particularly rapid growth in Asian populations [1]. Proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, and anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies represent MM therapy cornerstones. The introduction of these agents has markedly improved both progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) over the past decades [2]. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation provides further benefits to patients who respond well to induction therapy [3].

Although treatment progress has markedly improved the survival of patients with MM, the disease remains incurable. New therapeutic strategies are urgently warranted for patients previously treated for or resistant to proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, and anti-CD38 antibodies. Currently, the B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA), G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D, and Fc receptor-like 5 are the most extensively studied targets in relapsed refractory MM (RRMM) [4]. Notably, BCMA has demonstrated remarkable potential as an emerging therapeutic option for heavily pretreated MM. B-cell maturation antigen, also known as TNFRSF17 or CD269, belongs to the tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily. It is predominantly found in mature B cells, and its increased expression and activation are closely linked to MM [5], making it an ideal therapeutic target for MM treatment. Bispecific antibodies, antibody–drug conjugates, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies are major BCMA-targeted MM treatment platforms. These modalities have demonstrated impressive response rates in patients with heavily pretreated disease [6].

Compared with chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies, bispecific antibodies offer advantages regarding manufacturing simplicity and off-the-shelf availability. Elranatamab and teclistamab are US Food and Drug Administration-approved bispecific antibodies that have been widely used to treat RRMM. In the phase II MagnetisMM-3 trial, which included a heavily pretreated population with a median of five prior lines of therapy (100% triple-class exposed and 70.7% penta-refractory), elranatamab achieved an overall response rate of 61.0%, with 35.0% of patients attaining a complete response or better despite extensive prior treatment. [7]. Likewise, in the phase I–II MajesTEC-1 trial involving a similarly heavily pretreated cohort (median five prior lines; 100% triple-class exposed and 70.3% penta-refractory), teclistamab produced an overall response rate of 63.0%, with 39.4% achieving a complete response or deeper remission [8]. Nevertheless, clinical trials typically include selected patient populations that may not fully represent the real-world practice. Moreover, no direct comparative studies have been conducted between elranatamab and teclistamab in the RRMM setting.

To address this gap, we conducted a retrospective study using TriNetX. This study aimed to compare the time to the next treatment (TTNT), overall OS, and adverse events (AEs) in patients with RRMM receiving elranatamab or teclistamab monotherapy in real-world practice.

sec.title: Data Sources and Study Design
sec.p: This multinational, multicenter, retrospective cohort study used deidentified electronic health records from the TriNetX Global Research Network. The TriNetX platform harmonizes diagnoses, procedures, medications, and laboratory data from participating healthcare organizations into a common data model and provides only aggregated and deidentified analytic outputs; individual-level data are neither accessible nor downloadable. Adults (aged ≥ 18 years) with MM were identified using International Classification of Diseases and oncology codes mapped within the TriNetX platform. Two exposure cohorts were defined based on the first recorded administration of elranatamab or teclistamab (index date), and drug exposure was determined using RxNorm-mapped administration records. To approximate lines of therapy within the TriNetX network, eligible patients were required to have received one or more prior systemic anti-myeloma regimen before the index date. Administrations at ultra-low doses unlikely to represent therapeutic intent were excluded. Treatments were captured using standardized drug and procedure codes, and a prespecified line of therapy algorithm was applied to define sequential regimens and assign each patient’s lines of therapy at index. The full operational definitions and code lists are provided in Table 1 of the Electronic Supplementary Material.

To minimize baseline confounding, we used the TriNetX built-in logistic regression-based propensity score algorithm to perform 1:1 matching between the elranatamab and teclistamab cohorts. Covariates included in the propensity score model comprised age, sex, race/ethnicity, selected comorbidities (e.g., hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus), and key baseline laboratory parameters (hemoglobin, platelet count, albumin, β2-microglobulin, and estimated glomerular filtration rate). Continuous variables were discretized into categorical ranges for matching. Postmatching covariate balance was assessed using standardized mean differences; absolute values < 0.1 were considered acceptable. The matched cohorts were subsequently used for TTNT, OS, and safety analyses.

sec.title: Outcome Measurement
sec.p: The primary effectiveness endpoint was TTNT, defined as the duration from the index date to the earliest occurrence of either (i) any subsequent systemic antimyeloma therapy initiation, including proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, monoclonal antibodies, other bispecific antibodies, conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy, BCMA-directed chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, or autologous stem cell transplantation, or (ii) death. To minimize misclassifying overlapping administrations or early treatment adjustments as new therapy lines, the TTNT observation window spanned from day 14 to day 730 (2 years) following the index date.

The second primary effectiveness endpoint was OS, defined as the time from the index date to death from any cause, based on the TriNetX built-in “Deceased” flag. Overall survival was assessed from day 1 to day 1095 (3 years) following the index date; patients with a recorded death before day 1 were excluded from the OS analyses.

sec.title: Safety Analyses
sec.p: Safety analyses were performed in the same elranatamab and teclistamab cohorts. Cytokine-related toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), were identified using diagnostic codes for CRS and ICANS (both graded and ungraded) within a 1- to 15-day window after the index date. Administration of tocilizumab during this period was also incorporated as part of the CRS outcome definition. Hematological AEs were assessed during an acute window from day 1 to day 90 after index and included neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and their Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade ≥ 3 counterparts. These events were defined based on absolute neutrophil count, platelet count, and hemoglobin laboratory values using numerical thresholds aligned with the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grading and, when applicable, supplemented by relevant diagnosis codes.

Hypogammaglobulinemia was defined as a serum immunoglobulin G level < 4 g/L. As this cohort comprised heavily pretreated patients who often exhibited baseline hematologic and immunoglobulin abnormalities, hematologic- and immunoglobulin-related AE analyses were designed to reflect the overall burden rather than strictly incident toxicity. Therefore, patients with baseline abnormalities were retained, and both new and recurrent events occurring within the defined observation windows were included.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: Time-to-event outcomes (TTNT, OS, and, where applicable, time to first AE) were evaluated using Kaplan–Meier methods and compared between treatment groups using log-rank tests and Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Additionally, the cumulative risks and association measures (risk difference, risk ratio, and odds ratio) within predefined time windows were calculated. Patients without an event were censored at the date of their last recorded clinical encounter (“last fact”). All statistical tests were two-sided, and no formal adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied. Because the TriNetX built-in Cox proportional hazards model does not support stratified analyses following propensity score matching, the matched dataset was exported, and Kaplan–Meier survival analyses were performed independently for each predefined subgroup.

More than 196 million patients were screened, and 584,544 individuals with MM were identified. Patients with RRMM who received elranatamab (n = 191) or teclistamab (n = 1338) were included. sec.title: Treatment Outcome
sec.p:
The median TTNT was 11.0 months and 12.3 months in the elranatamab and teclistamab groups, respectively, with no statistically significant difference (p = 0.394) (Fig. 2A). Both groups exhibited comparable 3-year OS rates of 58.8% and 59.7% for elranatamab and teclistamab, respectively (p = 0.077) (Fig. 2B). An odds ratio analysis of the TTNT was conducted to identify patient subgroups that may derive differential benefits from elranatamab versus teclistamab (Fig. 3). No significant differences were observed between the elranatamab and teclistamab groups regarding age, sex, or ethnicity. Teclistamab was associated with improved TTNT among patients with a baseline platelet count < 100 × 103/µL (HR: 1.68; 95% CI 1.05–2.68; p = 0.029). Prior exposure to bortezomib (HR: 1.15; 95% CI 0.79–1.66; p = 0.479), lenalidomide (HR: 1.05; 95% CI 0.74–1.48; p = 0.794), daratumumab (HR: 0.95; 95% CI 0.67–1.35; p = 0.772), or autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HR: 0.83; 95% CI 0.54–1.25; p = 0.367) did not significantly affect the treatment effect. Notably, teclistamab conferred a more pronounced benefit among patients who had received more than five prior lines of therapy (HR: 1.92; 95% CI 1.16–3.20; p = 0.010).Fig. 2

sec.title: Adverse Events
sec.p:
Compared with elranatamab, a higher proportion of patients receiving teclistamab experienced ≥ grade 3 neutropenia (74.5% vs 84.6%, p = 0.015). Nonetheless, there were no significant differences in the incidence rates of sepsis (20.2% vs 18.1%, p = 0.600) or febrile neutropenia (11.7% vs 16.5%, p = 0.182) between the elranatamab and teclistamab groups (Table 2). Similarly, other hematologic AEs were comparable, including grade 3 anemia (32.4% vs 37.2%, p = 0.330) and grade 3 thrombocytopenia (23.9% vs 28.2%, p = 0.347). More patients treated with elranatamab experienced CRS of any grade than did those treated with teclistamab (45.2% vs 27.1%, p < 0.001), whereas the ICANS incidence was similar between the elranatamab and teclistamab cohorts (18.6% vs 13.3%, p = 0.159). Moreover, the infection rates were comparable, including those for pneumonia (20.7% vs 23.4%, p = 0.534), coronavirus disease 2019 (44.1% vs 47.3%, p = 0.535), influenza (39.4% vs 38.3%, p = 0.832), herpes zoster (6.9% vs 10.1%, p = 0.268), and cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (24.5% vs 18.6%, p = 0.168). sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this multicenter, propensity-matched, real-world cohort study, we compared the clinical efficacy and safety profiles of two BCMA-directed bispecific antibodies, elranatamab and teclistamab, in patients with RRMM. Elranatamab and teclistamab exhibited comparable clinical effectiveness, with similar median TTNT (11.0 vs 12.3 months; p = 0.394) and 3-year OS rates (58.8% vs 59.7%; p = 0.077). The subgroup analysis demonstrated no differential benefits across age, sex, or ethnicity. Nonetheless, teclistamab was associated with improved TTNT in patients with baseline thrombocytopenia and in those who had received more than five prior lines of therapy. Regarding safety, ≥ grade 3 neutropenia occurred more frequently with teclistamab, whereas CRS was more common with elranatamab. The incidences of ICANS and other hematological or infectious complications were similar between the groups, with no notable sepsis or pneumonia differences.

In this real-world setting, TTNT was employed as a pragmatic surrogate marker for PFS. Conceptually, these two measures are closely related; although the TTNT may slightly exceed real-world PFS, it is commonly used as a practical endpoint in observational research involving MM [9]. To externally validate our findings, we compared the outcomes of the elranatamab cohort with those reported in the MagnetisMM-1 trial [10]. In patients with RRMM treated with elranatamab, the median PFS in the MagnetisMM-1 trial was 11.8 months, which is comparable to the median TTNT of 11.0 months in our elranatamab cohort. For teclistamab, the median PFS was 11.3 months in the MajesTEC-1 study [8], comparable to the median TTNT of 12.3 months in our teclistamab cohort. Together, these indirect comparisons support the consistency and external validity of the findings.

To date, no studies have directly compared the efficacy of elranatamab and teclistamab in patients with RRMM. Our multinational, multicenter, retrospective cohort study, based on de-identified electronic health records from the TriNetX global research network, aimed to address this evidence gap. Specifically, elranatamab and teclistamab might be used interchangeably as both therapies demonstrated comparable clinical outcomes in patients with RRMM. [11]. However, a matching-adjusted indirect comparison of elranatamab versus teclistamab in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM by Mol et al. [12] revealed that elranatamab demonstrated a substantially superior response rate and PFS compared with teclistamab. Notably, this discrepancy may stem from the fundamental methodological differences between propensity score matching and matching-adjusted indirect comparisons. The former balances baseline characteristics using individual-level data from both treatment groups, enabling direct real-world comparisons, while the latter reweights individual-level data from one study to match aggregate characteristics from another when head-to-head data are unavailable, supporting indirect comparisons across separate trials [13].

Our subgroup outcomes were notable. Specifically, teclistamab was associated with improved TTNT in patients with baseline thrombocytopenia and in those who had received more than five prior lines of therapy. These heavily pretreated patients have limited therapeutic options and often diminished marrow reserves. The enhanced benefits observed in these subgroups may be related to differences in pharmacodynamics, tumor immune microenvironment modulation, or T-cell activation profiles between the two agents [14]. Nevertheless, these findings should be interpreted with caution, especially given the absence of statistically significant differences in OS and the lack of biological correlates in our dataset. Further mechanistic and prospective validation studies are warranted to clarify whether specific biological phenotypes or clinical characteristics differentially predict responses to individual BCMA-targeting bispecific antibodies.

The safety results of this real-world analysis merit further consideration. Higher rates of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia were observed in the teclistamab group (84.6% vs 74.5%; p = 0.015), whereas elranatamab was associated with a greater frequency of CRS of any grade (45.2% vs 27.1%; p < 0.001). A retrospective study by Dima et al. [15] reported a CRS incidence of 64% in patients with RRMM treated with teclistamab, which was substantially higher than that observed in our teclistamab cohort. A similar pattern was observed in the elranatamab cohort. The incidence of any-grade CRS in our analysis was 45.2%, lower than the 57.7% reported in the MagnetisMM-3 trial [7]. Beyond the differences in the study populations, the use of more intensive CRS prophylaxis, including high-dose corticosteroids and tocilizumab, might have contributed to the lower CRS incidence observed in our cohort [16]. Prophylactic tocilizumab reduces the incidence and severity of CRS in patients receiving BCMA bispecific antibodies while facilitating the administration of these therapies in an outpatient setting [17].

Despite differences in hematologic toxicity and cytokine-mediated inflammatory events, as well as a higher proportion of intravenous immunoglobulin use among patients treated with teclistamab compared with elranatamab (20.6% vs 12.8%; p = 0.047), no significant differences were observed in serious infectious complications, including pneumonia, febrile neutropenia, or sepsis. The comparable rates of hypogammaglobulinemia-associated viral and opportunistic infections suggest that both therapies cause substantial immune suppression, likely reflecting the on-target plasma cell depletion and T-cell exhaustion effects common to BCMA-directed immunotherapies. Therefore, vigilant infection surveillance, immunoglobulin monitoring, and prophylactic strategies are critical in clinical practice. Currently, routine prophylaxis against herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, along with monthly intravenous immunoglobulin replacement for immunoparesis, is recommended for patients with RRMM treated with BCMA bispecific antibodies [18]. This prophylactic strategy is consistent with our findings, in which the incidence of pneumonia and herpes zoster was acceptable. Notably, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia incidence in our cohort was extremely low.

Cytomegalovirus prophylaxis represents a gray area in patients with RRMM treated with BCMA bispecific antibodies, owing to the limited clinical trial experience to date [19]. The most available evidence regarding CMV surveillance and prophylaxis comes from allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients [20, 21], rather than from patients receiving BCMA bispecific antibodies. Here, CMV infection rates were as high as 24.5% and 18.6% in the elranatamab and teclistamab cohorts, respectively, indicating that even without a standardized CMV prophylaxis protocol, close surveillance remains essential for patients with RRMM receiving BCMA bispecific antibodies.

Nevertheless, this study has some limitations. First, the retrospective nature of this study introduces potential residual confounding factors despite propensity score matching. Important biological markers, including cytogenetic risk status, tumor burden, soluble BCMA levels, and functional immune indices, were unavailable in the dataset and could have affected treatment response. In addition, a de-identified dataset does not allow determination of the individual patient International Staging System or Revised International Staging System stage. Second, although TTNT is a meaningful real-world endpoint, it may be influenced by physician decision making, patient preferences, and institutional practice patterns. Because TTNT captures the interval to initiation of subsequent therapy, and given the retrospective design and inherent limitations of the TriNetX database, it should be interpreted as a pragmatic measure of disease control rather than equivalent to progression-free survival. Third, AE identification was based on structured diagnostic codes and laboratory-derived thresholds, without manual adjudication or uniform grading. This may have led to an underestimation or misclassification of toxicity severity. In particular, identification of CRS relied on diagnostic codes and tocilizumab administration, which may preferentially capture clinically significant events and underestimate lower-grade cases. Mild or transient CRS episodes that do not prompt coding or specific treatment may therefore be under-represented, and this potential under-ascertainment should be considered when interpreting cross-cohort comparisons. Additionally, the relatively short follow-up period for some patients, especially those treated more recently, may limit the interpretation of the long-term durability and late toxicities. Another important consideration is the multiplicity of subgroup analyses. Although exploratory analyses provide valuable hypothesis-generating insights, the lack of multiplicity adjustment means that some observed associations may reflect chance rather than true biological interactions. Therefore, the subgroup findings should be interpreted cautiously and validated in future controlled studies. Randomized controlled studies are required to directly compare the efficacy and safety of elranatamab and teclistamab in patients with RRMM.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This real-world propensity score-matched analysis suggests that elranatamab and teclistamab provide comparable overall clinical efficacy in heavily pretreated RRMM, with differential toxicity patterns and potential subgroup-dependent treatment benefit differences. Both agents remain valuable therapeutic options, and treatment selection may be informed by patient-specific clinical factors, risk-benefit considerations, and logistical accessibility. Future mechanistic, biomarker-driven, and prospective head-to-head studies are warranted to refine the therapeutic sequencing and optimize outcomes in this challenging patient population.

notes.p: Chieh-Lin Jerry Teng received honoraria and consulting fees from Novartis, Roche, Pfizer, Takeda, Johnson and Johnson, Amgen, BMS Celgene, TTY, and MSD. notes.title: Ethics Approval
notes.p: Participant details were de-identified, and study was conducted according to the current version of the Declaration of Helsinki. The Institutional Review Board of Taichung Veterans General Hospital approved the study (CE251005A).

notes.title: Consent to Participate
notes.p: The Institutional Review Board of Taichung Veterans General Hospital agreed to waive the requirement for obtaining informed consent from the participants because of the retrospective nature of the study.

notes.title: Availability of Data and Material
notes.p: The datasets used and/or analyzed during the current study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

notes.title: Author Contributions
notes.p: Y-CW: conceptualization, methodology, investigation, writing (review and editing). P-HL: conceptualization, methodology, investigation. C-HL: conceptualization, investigation, formal analysis, writing (review and editing). Y-CS: methodology, investigation, writing (review and editing). C‐LJT: conceptualization, supervision, writing (review and editing). All authors gave final approval of the manuscript.
